name: permission-wildcarding
description: Reduces approval friction in Claude Code and Codex with history-based learning, reviewed permission changes, policy recovery, shell guidance, memory diagnostics and recall. Codex uses native prefix rules and reviewed MCP settings. Codex support remains experimental.

permissionWildcarding.backupMirrorPath.markdownDescription: Where to mirror the allow/deny high-water-mark backup, in addition to `~/.claude/backups/allow-list.latest.json`. Empty uses `~/.permission-wildcarding/allow-list.latest.json`. The primary copy lives inside `~/.claude`, so it cannot survive that directory being recreated rather than merely rewritten — the mirror is the copy that can. Set it to a path on another volume to survive more than a reset. Written second and best-effort, so a bad path can never cost you the primary backup; restore reads the primary first and falls back to the mirror. Machine-scoped, so a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` cannot choose where your allow and deny lists are written; set it in user settings.

permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.enabled.markdownDescription: Incrementally correlate Claude Code and Codex shell history on startup, on transcript changes, and during periodic reconciliation. Confirmed successes add evidence, failures are retained as negative evidence, and unanswered calls are ignored. Raw transcript arguments and absolute transcript paths are never saved in Auto Learn state. **AI Acolyte: Toggle Auto Learn** and the Auto Learn card's button switch it in your user settings. Off stops the extension's background scans only: Codex's after-turn Stop hook and `wildcard-perms --learn` do not read this setting. A workspace may only make this stricter: it can turn Auto Learn off, never on when your user setting has it off.

enumDescriptions: Learn counts only; never propose or apply policy.
Learn continuously and show candidates for review (recommended).
Automatically apply only deterministic, suffix-closed read-only candidates after the success threshold and with zero confirmed failures.
permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.mode.markdownDescription: Auto Learn operating mode. `auto-safe` requires a suffix-closed read-only prefix, judged on the *pattern* rather than the observed command: an applied `Bash(<root> *)` also matches `<root> ... > <path>`, and no allow pattern can exclude a redirection. Auto-safe is therefore limited to roots where no argument can reach stdout — `echo`, `printf`, `Write-*`, `basename`, `dirname`, `Get-Date` and `git cat-file` are excluded, along with destructive, administrative, credential-related, network-capable, package-install, wrapper, and ambiguous candidates. All remain review-only. Accepted residual: an auto-safe root can still truncate a path with fixed content (`whoami > f`), so keep catastrophic paths in `permissions.deny`. A workspace may only make this stricter: a workspace or folder value can lower the mode, and one above your user setting is ignored (the Acolyte output channel says so once). Raising it is always your user setting.

permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.successT.markdownDescription: Successful correlated executions required before a normalized command family becomes eligible for automatic safe application. A workspace may only make this stricter: it can raise the threshold, never lower it below your user setting.

permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.interval.markdownDescription: Periodic reconciliation interval in minutes. File watchers usually learn sooner; reconciliation catches events missed while VS Code was suspended.

permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.debounce.markdownDescription: How long to wait after transcript activity settles before a watcher-driven scan runs, in seconds. Higher = fewer scans during active work (the periodic reconcile is the backstop). Auto Learn reads incrementally, so a later scan just processes a larger batch — nothing is lost.

enumDescriptions: Write the dedicated user rule file at `~/.codex/rules/permission-wildcarding.rules`.
Learn from Codex history but do not write Codex rules.
permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.codexSco.markdownDescription:
Where validated generated Codex rules are written. Codex loads rules at startup, so restart Codex after a rule change.

`workspace` is **withdrawn**: its trust model could not be stated, because VS Code workspace trust, this setting and Codex's own project trust are three different decisions and only the last governs whether Codex loads a workspace rule file. A settings file that still says `workspace` is accepted, but Codex rule export stays OFF and the Auto Learn card says so. To remove rules an older release wrote into a repository: `wildcard-perms --codex-workspace-rules remove`.

A workspace may only make this stricter: it can turn export `off`, never back to `user` when your user setting says `off`.

permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.codexExe.markdownDescription: Command name or absolute path of the Codex CLI. The extension runs it without asking: `codex execpolicy check` (Auto Learn never writes a Codex rule unless this validation succeeds), `--version` for the dashboard's version line, and `app-server` to ask which project rule folders Codex trusts. Machine-scoped, so a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` cannot point it at a binary of its own; set it in user settings.

permissionWildcarding.autoLearn.workerTi.markdownDescription: How long one Auto Learn worker operation (a scan, apply or undo) may run before the extension stops waiting for it, in seconds. `0` disables the deadline, which attaching a debugger to the worker needs. The default clears Auto Learn's own 180-second child-process timeouts by a minute: it is a backstop for a worker stuck in a synchronous filesystem call, such as a dead network mount, not a budget. Raise it only if a legitimately slow scan is being cut off. A change applies to the next operation without a reload. Machine-scoped, so a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` cannot switch it off. While unset, `PERMISSION_WILDCARDING_WORKER_TIMEOUT_MS` in the environment still applies.

permissionWildcarding.localDrain.enabled.markdownDescription: Promote portable approvals from each workspace's `.claude/settings.local.json` — the file Claude Code writes an "always approve" into — up to user-scope `settings.json`, then drop the local entries user scope now covers. Only clean command families move (`Bash(<root> *)`, `Tool(<root> <sub> *)`); script blobs, absolute-path executables, MCP tools and file/web families stay local. A local entry is removed only after its promotion is verified in `settings.json`, so a pruned entry is always still granted. Refused while legacy blanket `Bash(*)` and `PowerShell(*)` grants remain, because they cover every local entry. Untrusted workspaces are read-only. A workspace may only make this stricter: it can turn the automatic drain off, never on when your user setting has it off.

permissionWildcarding.guidance.enabled.markdownDescription: Maintain a managed shell-style block in each installed agent's user instruction file (`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` and `~/.codex/AGENTS.md`). Simple commands make Claude approval patterns and Codex argv-prefix rules easier to reuse. Codex may split simple shell chains; expansions, redirections, and other complex syntax can instead require a rule for the complete wrapper. Script files need their own approval. Turning this off removes the managed block and preserves your text. Machine-scoped, because it writes your global instruction files: a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` can neither add the block nor strip it; set it in user settings.

permissionWildcarding.gates.enabled.markdownDescription: Maintain a second managed block holding your own **standing orders**, compiled out of your Claude Code file-memory. `recall.py --gates-compile` lifts the `<!-- gate -->` section from every memory marked `scope: global` into `~/.claude/gates.generated.md`, and this installs it into each agent's instruction file. Why it needs to be resident: the memory index is a list of one-line hooks, so the enforceable half of a rule sits in a file that only loads if a recall surfaces it — which never happens for a rule you are already breaking, because nothing triggers the lookup. Reference material is fine on demand; policy is not. Installing is a file read and runs on activation; compiling spawns python, an explicit action until the block is installed and then again after each memory edit. Marker-fenced separately from the shell-style block, so turning either off leaves the other byte-identical. To retire or restore one gate at a time instead, run **AI Acolyte: Manage memory gates…**: it edits and recompiles either way, and installs its change only while this is on, which it never changes. Machine-scoped, because it writes your global instruction files: a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` can neither install the block nor remove it; set it in user settings.

permissionWildcarding.openThreads.enable.markdownDescription: Maintain a third managed block, **open threads**, in each agent's instruction file. `recall.py --threads-compile` lists every memory whose frontmatter `status:` is `open`, `awaiting`, `blocked` or `deferred`, with the text of its `<!-- status -->` block, into `~/.claude/open-threads.generated.md`, and this installs it. While `MEMORY.md` is past 140 lines, 12000 bytes or a 300-character line, the block also carries an INDEX line telling every new session to compact it. Status then has a home outside the index, whose first 200 lines are all Claude Code loads. The compile runs on its own: after a memory edit that can change the list, on activation when there is anything to say, and when this is turned on. Off removes the block and nothing compiles or installs it. Machine-scoped, because it writes your global instruction files: a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` can neither install the block nor remove it; set it in user settings.

permissionWildcarding.claudeStripModelCh.markdownDescription: Once per new Claude Code binary, check whether its known-safe environment variables (the `NAME=value` prefixes Claude Code strips before it matches an allow rule) are still the Claude Code 2.1.296 list AI Acolyte's generalizer models. It runs about 30 seconds after activation, on a worker thread, and only when the installed binary's path, size or modification time has changed since the last check. A difference shows one warning per binary; nothing is ever edited, so a list change still needs an AI Acolyte release. Machine-scoped: a workspace value is ignored.

permissionWildcarding.memory.enabled.markdownDescription: Lint the Claude Code file-memory index (`MEMORY.md`) for bloat and broken links: a status-bar gauge plus editor diagnostics on over-budget hook lines and links to missing files.

permissionWildcarding.memory.dir.markdownDescription: Absolute path to a specific memory dir to lint (the folder containing `MEMORY.md`). Leave empty to auto-discover every `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/MEMORY.md`. It is also the corpus the recall index is built from and the one `--gates-compile` lifts into your global instruction files, so it is machine-scoped: a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` cannot point it at memories of its own; set it in user settings.

permissionWildcarding.memory.lineBudget.markdownDescription: Max **characters in one** `MEMORY.md` line (any line, counted in characters, not UTF-16 units) before it's flagged. (This is a width limit for a single line, not a limit on how many lines the file may have — that's `#permissionWildcarding.memory.maxLines#`.) Hooks over this are drifting into changelog territory — move the detail into the memory file or the project repo. This tunes the editor gauge, not the MEMORY.md guard: the guard hook always uses 300.

permissionWildcarding.memory.maxLines.markdownDescription: How many **lines** of `MEMORY.md` Claude Code actually loads. It reads the first 200 lines (or 25 KB, whichever comes first) and drops the rest **without reporting it**, so anything past the cap is silently absent from every session. This is the limit that usually arrives first, because the index grows by roughly a line per project while its byte count barely moves. Change it only if the loader's cap changes.

permissionWildcarding.memory.totalBudget.markdownDescription: Byte budget for the whole always-loaded `MEMORY.md` index before the gauge warns. This tunes the editor gauge, not the MEMORY.md guard: the guard hook always uses 12000.

permissionWildcarding.memory.recallScrip.markdownDescription: Absolute path to a `memory/recall.py` to use instead of the bundled one. The script powers the dashboard Memory card's **Rebuild recall index** button (a CPU bge-small re-embed of the memory dir). Leave empty to use the copy bundled with the extension (or, in a development checkout, the checkout's own); no workspace folder is searched. The passive CPU-LLM status probe works either way. Machine-scoped, because the extension runs this script: a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` cannot point it at a script of its own; set it in user settings.
